title: 11 — Azure Data Services (SQL, Cosmos DB, Redis)
html:
11 — Azure Data Services (SQL, Cosmos DB, Redis)

The three data services a .NET developer meets most. General relational and NoSQL theory is in the main KB (files 10 and 11); this file is the Azure-specific layer.

1. Azure SQL — which flavour?

Option What it is Use when
Azure SQL Database ⭐ A single PaaS database. Fully managed, auto-patched, auto-backed-up Almost every new application
Elastic pool Many databases sharing purchased capacity Multi-tenant with database-per-tenant and uneven load
SQL Managed Instance Near-100% SQL Server surface: SQL Agent, cross-database queries, CLR, Service Broker Lift-and-shift where the app needs instance-level features
SQL Server on a VM IaaS — you own everything You need a specific version, OS access, or unsupported features

💡 Default to Azure SQL Database. Reach for Managed Instance only when a specific instance-level feature blocks you — you're taking on more cost and a slower service.

1.1 Purchasing models

DTU model vCore model ⭐
Unit A blended CPU/IO/memory measure Explicit cores + memory + storage
Tiers Basic, Standard, Premium General Purpose, Business Critical, Hyperscale
Transparency Opaque You can reason about it
Azure Hybrid Benefit ✘ ✔ Reuse on-prem licences
Verdict Legacy — simple but unreasonable Use this for anything new

vCore service tiers:

Tier Storage Latency HA Use
General Purpose Remote premium storage ~5–10 ms IO Compute+storage separated; failover restarts compute ⭐ Most workloads
Business Critical Local SSD ~1–2 ms IO An Always On availability group with 3 replicas + a free readable secondary Latency-sensitive OLTP
Hyperscale Distributed page servers Fast Rapid scaling, up to 100 TB, near-instant restore Very large databases

Compute tiers: Provisioned (fixed vCores, predictable) vs Serverless (auto-scales within a range and auto-pauses when idle — great for dev/test and intermittent workloads). ⚠️ Serverless auto-pause means the first connection after idle takes ~30–60 seconds to resume; never use it for a production API without understanding that.

1.2 ⭐ Connecting with a managed identity — no password

// Connection string with NO credentials
"Server=tcp:sql-shop-prod.database.windows.net,1433;
 Initial Catalog=shop;
 Authentication=Active Directory Default;
 Encrypt=True;TrustServerCertificate=False;Connection Timeout=30;"

-- Run ONCE, connected as an Entra admin on the server (not a SQL login)
CREATE USER [app-shop-api-prod] FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER;   -- the managed identity's display name
ALTER ROLE db_datareader ADD MEMBER [app-shop-api-prod];
ALTER ROLE db_datawriter ADD MEMBER [app-shop-api-prod];
GRANT EXECUTE ON SCHEMA::dbo TO [app-shop-api-prod];      -- if it calls stored procedures
-- ⚠️ Never db_owner for an application identity.

⚠️ Gotchas: the server must have an Entra administrator configured; for a user-assigned identity you must also supply the client id (User Id=<clientId> in the connection string or via SqlAuthenticationProvider); and each deployment slot has its own identity, so create a database user for the staging slot too.

1.3 Resilience in EF Core

builder.Services.AddDbContextPool<AppDbContext>(options =>
    options.UseSqlServer(connectionString, sql =>
    {
        sql.EnableRetryOnFailure(
            maxRetryCount: 5,
            maxRetryDelay: TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10),
            errorNumbersToAdd: [1205]);          // include deadlocks
        sql.CommandTimeout(30);
    }));

⚠️ Azure SQL is a multi-tenant service and will drop connections during failovers, maintenance, and throttling. Transient-fault retry is not optional — it's the difference between a maintenance window being invisible and being an incident.

⚠️ With EnableRetryOnFailure, user-initiated transactions must use the execution strategy, or EF throws:

var strategy = db.Database.CreateExecutionStrategy();
await strategy.ExecuteAsync(async () =>
{
    await using var tx = await db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync(ct);
    // ... work ...
    await tx.CommitAsync(ct);
});

Connection pooling: ADO.NET pools per distinct connection string (default max 100). ⚠️ Pool exhaustion presents as "Timeout expired. The timeout period elapsed prior to obtaining a connection from the pool" and is almost always a leaked connection (a missing using) or a long-running query holding connections — not an undersized pool.

1.4 Performance and operations

Tool Use
Query Performance Insight (portal) ⭐ Top queries by CPU/duration/execution count. Start here
Query Store Plan history, regression detection, forced plans
Automatic tuning Auto-create/drop indexes and force last-good plans. 💡 Enable FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN — it fixes parameter-sniffing regressions automatically
Intelligent Insights Diagnostic log of detected performance problems
sys.dm_db_resource_stats Actual DTU/vCore utilisation over the last hour 
-- Am I hitting the tier's ceiling?
SELECT TOP 60 end_time,
       avg_cpu_percent, avg_data_io_percent, avg_log_write_percent,
       max_worker_percent, max_session_percent
FROM sys.dm_db_resource_stats ORDER BY end_time DESC;

⚠️ Azure SQL throttles when you hit the tier limits — you'll see waits, timeouts, and error 10928/10929. Check avg_*_percent before assuming your query is bad; sometimes the tier genuinely is too small.

1.5 Business continuity

Feature RPO / RTO Notes
Automated backups PITR to any point in the retention window (7–35 days) On by default. Full weekly, differential ~12h, log every 5–10 min
Long-term retention Weekly/monthly/yearly for up to 10 years For compliance
Zone redundancy ~0 / seconds Survives a datacentre failure. 💡 Enable in production
Active geo-replication Seconds / manual failover Up to 4 readable secondaries in other regions
Failover groups Seconds / automatic ⭐ Adds a stable listener endpoint so the connection string doesn't change on failover
Geo-restore Hours From geo-redundant backups; the fallback of last resort

💡 Failover groups over raw geo-replication — the listener endpoint means your application doesn't need to know a failover happened. ⚠️ Test the restore. A backup you've never restored is a hypothesis.

1.6 Security

  • Entra authentication only where possible; disable SQL authentication.
  • Private endpoint + Public network access: Disabled, with the privatelink.database.windows.net DNS zone.
  • TDE is on by default; Always Encrypted for column-level protection where even a DBA must not see the values.
  • Dynamic data masking for non-production access; row-level security for multi-tenant isolation.
  • Auditing to Log Analytics, and Microsoft Defender for SQL (vulnerability assessment + threat detection).
  • ⚠️ "Allow Azure services to access this server" opens the firewall to every Azure tenant, not just yours. Use a private endpoint or explicit rules.

2. Cosmos DB

Globally distributed, multi-model NoSQL with SLA-backed single-digit-millisecond latency. Powerful and easy to misuse.

2.1 The hierarchy and the cost model

Account  (choose the API at creation — ⚠️ IRREVERSIBLE)
└── Database        ← throughput can be shared here
    └── Container   ← the unit of scale; throughput usually provisioned here
        └── Items   ← JSON documents, grouped into logical partitions

Request Units (RU/s) are the currency. Every operation costs RUs based on the work done: a 1 KB point read ≈ 1 RU; a write ≈ 5+ RU; a query depends entirely on how many items it examines.

Throughput mode Use
Provisioned (manual) Predictable load. You pay for the ceiling
Autoscale ⭐ Scales 10%–100% of a maximum. Costs ~1.5× the manual rate per RU but usually cheaper overall for variable load
Serverless Pay per operation. Dev/test and genuinely intermittent workloads. Has lower limits 🔄

⚠️ A Cosmos container left at a load-test RU setting is one of the classic Azure surprise bills. Set budget alerts and review provisioned RUs monthly.

2.2 ⭐ Partitioning — the decision that determines everything

The partition key is chosen at container creation and determines physical distribution. Choose badly and you cannot fix it without migrating the data.

A good partition key has:

  1. High cardinality — many distinct values.
  2. Even distribution of both storage and request volume (no celebrity skew).
  3. Presence in your most common queries — otherwise every query is a cross-partition scan.
  4. A logical partition under 20 GB 🔄 — the hard limit.
// ✔ Queries are almost always scoped to a portfolio, and there are many portfolios
new ContainerProperties("holdings", partitionKeyPath: "/portfolioId")

// ❌ /type — a handful of values, so a few enormous, hot partitions
// ❌ /date — today's partition takes all writes (a hot partition)
// ❌ /id   — perfect distribution, but every query that isn't a point read fans out

💡 Synthetic keys when no single property works: "tenantId-yyyyMM" gives distribution and bounded partition size. Hierarchical partition keys (up to 3 levels, e.g. /tenantId + /portfolioId) are the modern answer to "my natural key exceeds 20 GB" 🔄.

// ⭐ A point read: PartitionKey + id. ~1 RU, single-digit ms. Always prefer this.
var response = await container.ReadItemAsync<Holding>(
    id: holdingId, partitionKey: new PartitionKey(portfolioId), cancellationToken: ct);

// ✔ Single-partition query
var query = new QueryDefinition("SELECT * FROM c WHERE c.instrumentCode = @code")
    .WithParameter("@code", code);
using var iterator = container.GetItemQueryIterator<Holding>(query,
    requestOptions: new QueryRequestOptions { PartitionKey = new PartitionKey(portfolioId) });

// ⚠️ Cross-partition — fans out to EVERY physical partition. Expensive and slow at scale.
using var crossPartition = container.GetItemQueryIterator<Holding>(
    new QueryDefinition("SELECT * FROM c WHERE c.instrumentCode = @code").WithParameter("@code", code));

🧪 Always log response.RequestCharge in development. It's the only way to learn what your queries actually cost — and a query that costs 400 RUs instead of 4 is invisible until the 429s start.

2.3 Consistency levels

Level Guarantee Cost
Strong Linearizable Highest RU, highest latency, limits multi-region writes
Bounded staleness Lag bounded by K versions or T seconds High
Session ⭐ Read-your-own-writes per client session The default, and right for most apps
Consistent prefix Order preserved, but possibly stale Low
Eventual Converges eventually Lowest RU

💡 Session consistency is the sweet spot — the user always sees their own writes, at a fraction of the cost of Strong. Choose deliberately and write down why.

2.4 Other things to know

  • Change feed — an ordered log of inserts and updates per partition. ⭐ The foundation for materialised views, event-driven architectures, and Cosmos-triggered Functions. (⚠️ It does not capture deletes — use soft deletes with a TTL.)
  • TTL — per-container or per-item automatic expiry. Excellent for sessions, caches, and event data.
  • Indexing policy — everything is indexed by default, which costs RUs on every write. 💡 Exclude paths you never filter on; it can cut write RUs substantially.
  • Multi-region — add read regions for latency; multi-region writes require a conflict-resolution policy (last-write-wins by default) and you must understand what you're accepting.
  • Managed identity for data-plane access with Cosmos RBAC — no account keys.

⚠️ 429 (Request rate too large) means you've exceeded provisioned RUs. The SDK retries automatically with the server's retry-after, but sustained 429s mean either under-provisioning or an inefficient query pattern (usually cross-partition queries or a hot partition). Fix the cause, don't just raise the RUs.

3. Azure Cache for Redis

Tier 🔄 Notes
Basic Single node, no SLA. Dev only
Standard Two-node replicated, 99.9% SLA
Premium ⭐ Clustering, persistence, VNet/private endpoint, zone redundancy, geo-replication
Enterprise / Enterprise Flash Redis Enterprise modules (RediSearch, RedisJSON), active-active, NVMe tier

3.1 Using it from .NET

// StackExchange.Redis: the multiplexer is EXPENSIVE and thread-safe — ONE per app
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IConnectionMultiplexer>(sp =>
{
    var config = ConfigurationOptions.Parse(cacheConnectionString);
    config.AbortOnConnectFail = false;      // ⭐ keep retrying instead of failing at startup
    config.ConnectRetry = 3;
    config.ConnectTimeout = 5000;
    config.SyncTimeout = 5000;
    return ConnectionMultiplexer.Connect(config);
});

// Or the distributed-cache abstraction
builder.Services.AddStackExchangeRedisCache(options =>
{
    options.Configuration = cacheConnectionString;
    options.InstanceName = "shop:";
});

// ⭐ .NET 9 HybridCache: L1 in-memory + L2 Redis, with stampede protection built in
builder.Services.AddHybridCache(o => o.DefaultEntryOptions = new()
{
    Expiration = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5),
    LocalCacheExpiration = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30),
});

⚠️ Creating a ConnectionMultiplexer per request will exhaust connections and destroy performance. It is the single most common Redis mistake in .NET.

3.2 Operational rules

Rule Why
Every key gets a TTL unless there's a documented reason Unbounded growth is the standard Redis incident
Set maxmemory-policy to allkeys-lru for a cache ⚠️ The default (volatile-lru/noeviction) can start rejecting writes when full
Never KEYS * in production Redis is single-threaded — it blocks everything. Use SCAN
Avoid large values A 50 MB value blocks the server while it's transferred
Key naming: app:entity:id:version shop:portfolio:42:v3 — bumping the version invalidates a whole class atomically
Pipeline/batch 100 round trips at 0.5 ms = 50 ms; batched ≈ 1 ms
Cluster mode: use hash tags {portfolio:42}:holdings and {portfolio:42}:meta co-locate for multi-key ops
⚠️ Don't use Redis as a lock for correctness Without fencing tokens it isn't safe under GC pauses and clock drift. Use a database constraint

Capacity planning: size for the working set plus overhead (replication, fragmentation — plan for ~1.5× your data), and watch evicted keys, used memory percentage, cache hit rate, server load, and connected clients.

⚠️ Plan for the cache being empty. If your database can't take 100% of traffic during a Redis restart or failover, the cache is an availability dependency, not an optimisation. That's a design decision you should make consciously.

4. Choosing between them

flowchart TD
    A[New dataset] --> B{Relationships, transactions,<br/>and ad-hoc queries?}
    B -->|Yes| SQL[(⭐ Azure SQL Database)]
    B -->|No| C{Access pattern?}
    C -->|Point lookup by a known key,<br/>massive scale, global| COS[(Cosmos DB)]
    C -->|Ephemeral, sub-ms, cache/session| RED[(Redis)]
    C -->|Blobs, files, documents| BLOB[(Blob Storage)]
    C -->|Analytics over billions of rows| SYN[(Synapse / Fabric / Databricks)]
    C -->|Append-only telemetry| ADX[(Data Explorer)]

💡 Default to Azure SQL unless you have a specific, evidenced reason. Modern Azure SQL handles JSON, full-text search, graph, and geospatial — one operational surface instead of five. Polyglot persistence is real, but every extra store is another thing to back up, secure, monitor, upgrade, and hire for.

⚠️ The classic mis-selection: choosing Cosmos DB for relational data "because it scales". Six months later you're doing application-side joins, maintaining referential integrity by hand, paying for cross-partition queries, and you can't change the partition key.

5. Checklist

Azure SQL

  • vCore model; tier and size chosen from measured utilisation
  • Entra authentication with managed identity; SQL auth disabled; not db_owner
  • Database users created for every slot's identity
  • EnableRetryOnFailure configured; execution strategy used around manual transactions
  • Zone redundancy in production; failover group if there's a cross-region RTO
  • Private endpoint + DNS zone; "Allow Azure services" off
  • Auditing to Log Analytics; Defender for SQL enabled
  • PITR retention set; a restore actually tested
  • Query Store on; FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN enabled
  • Alerts on DTU/vCore %, deadlocks, failed connections, storage %

Cosmos DB

  • Partition key: high cardinality, even distribution, present in common queries, partitions < 20 GB
  • Point reads used where possible; cross-partition queries identified and justified
  • RequestCharge logged in development
  • Autoscale configured with a sensible maximum; budget alert set
  • Indexing policy trimmed to what you actually filter on
  • Consistency level chosen deliberately (Session unless proven otherwise)
  • TTL configured for ephemeral data
  • Managed identity + Cosmos RBAC; account keys disabled
  • 429 rate monitored — treated as a design signal, not just a throughput one

Redis

  • IConnectionMultiplexer registered as a singleton
  • Premium tier with zone redundancy if it's on the critical path
  • maxmemory-policy = allkeys-lru; every key has a TTL
  • No KEYS in production code; no large values
  • Key naming convention with a version prefix
  • The origin can survive a cold cache, or that dependency is documented and accepted
  • Hit rate, evictions, memory %, and server load monitored

🔍 Questions to test yourself

  • Azure SQL Database vs Managed Instance? A single managed database vs near-full SQL Server instance surface (Agent, cross-database queries, CLR). Default to Database; use MI only when a specific instance feature blocks you.
  • Why is transient-fault retry mandatory on Azure SQL? It's a multi-tenant PaaS: failovers, maintenance and throttling drop connections routinely. Without retry, planned maintenance becomes a user-visible incident.
  • How do you pick a Cosmos partition key? High cardinality, even distribution of storage and traffic, present in the dominant query, and keeping logical partitions under 20 GB — and it's immutable, so getting it wrong means a data migration.
  • What is an RU, and why did my bill explode? The normalised cost of an operation. Usually cross-partition queries, an over-broad indexing policy, or provisioned throughput left at a test value.
  • Which Cosmos consistency level and why? Session by default — read-your-own-writes per client at a fraction of Strong's cost and latency.
  • What breaks if Redis goes down? If the answer isn't "we degrade to the database and stay up", the cache is an availability dependency and needs the origin capacity-planned for a cold start.
